claims.text: MaxKernel is evaluated on TPU v6e using JaxBench, a suite of 50 workloads containing 17 operators from widely used language-model architectures and 33 fused operators adapted from KernelBench.
claims.poster_quote: MaxKernel is evaluated on TPU v6e using JaxBench, a suite of 50 workloads containing 17 operators from widely used language-model architectures and 33 fused operators adapted from KernelBench.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We systematically evaluate the MaxKernel system on JaxBench [16], a curated suite of 50 diverse hardware-accelerated workloads. This benchmark comprises 17 widely used operators adapted from popular LLM architectures (e.g., complex attention mechanisms) and 33 fused operators adapted from the KernelBench dataset.
claims.reason: Section 3, Experiments and Results, confirms the evaluation of MaxKernel on TPU v6e using JaxBench, which includes 17 operators from language-model architectures and 33 fused operators from KernelBench.

claims.text: Tasks span attention, dense and sparse linear algebra, loss functions, and highly fused operations.
claims.poster_quote: Tasks span attention, dense and sparse linear algebra, loss functions, and highly fused operations.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Spanning attention variants, dense and sparse linear algebra, complex loss functions, and highly fused operations, JaxBench provides a rigorous testbed to evaluate MaxKernel’s capability for end-to-end kernel generation and hardware-specific optimization.
claims.reason: Section 3, Experiments and Results, explicitly states that the tasks span attention, dense and sparse linear algebra, loss functions, and highly fused operations.

claims.text: MaxKernel models kernel optimization as a SearchGraph in which each node contains source code, an optimization plan, correctness results, latency, and speedup.
claims.poster_quote: MaxKernel models kernel optimization as a SearchGraph in which each node contains source code, an optimization plan, correctness results, latency, and speedup.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The kernel generation process is modeled as a formal search problem where the orchestrator maintains a SearchGraph. Each node represents a specific state of the kernel produced by the auto agent worker, encompassing the source code, the optimization plan, and empirical evaluation metrics (e.g., correctness and speedup).
claims.reason: Section 2.5, Graph-Based Autonomous Search, confirms that MaxKernel models kernel optimization as a SearchGraph, with nodes containing source code, optimization plans, correctness results, latency, and speedup.

claims.text: Every node expansion launches a separate Auto-agent session, reducing context overflow and allowing persistent recovery from interrupted searches.
claims.poster_quote: Every node expansion launches a separate Auto-agent session, reducing context overflow and allowing persistent recovery from interrupted searches.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Each worker instantiates the Auto Agent to independently apply a new optimization strategy, compile, test, and profile the resulting kernel variations in parallel. [...] This graph-based abstraction [...] allows the system to recover gracefully from unexpected halts via the persistent graph state.
claims.reason: Section 2.5, Graph-Based Autonomous Search, confirms that every node expansion launches a separate Auto-agent session, reducing context overflow and enabling recovery from interrupted searches.

claims.text: Large Language Models can help generate kernels, but zero-shot or few-shot generation lacks the real-time compiler and hardware feedback required for reliable optimization.
claims.poster_quote: Large Language Models can help generate kernels, but zero-shot or few-shot generation lacks the real-time compiler and hardware feedback required for reliable optimization.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Standard zero-shot or few-shot LLM approaches need to be augmented with real-time compiler feedback due to the rigidity of accelerator APIs, strict memory constraints, and opaque low-level compiler errors.
claims.reason: Section 1, Introduction, explicitly states that zero-shot or few-shot LLM approaches lack real-time compiler and hardware feedback for reliable optimization.

claims.text: MaxKernel addresses this gap with a multi-agent framework that combines planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, autotuning, and XProf-based profiling in closed feedback loops.
claims.poster_quote: MaxKernel addresses this gap with a multi-agent framework that combines planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, autotuning, and XProf-based profiling in closed feedback loops.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: MaxKernel is a modular, agent-based system that tackles complex kernel optimization by breaking it into focused tasks. [...] The architecture relies on a suite of specialized sub-agents dedicated to planning, implementation, testing, autotuning, and profiling.
claims.reason: Section 2, System Architecture & Agent Paradigms, confirms that MaxKernel addresses the gap with a multi-agent framework combining planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, autotuning, and profiling.

claims.text: Metrics include compilation rate, correctness rate, geometric mean speedup over XLA with regressions floored at 1.0×, and fast-p: the fraction of tasks that are correct and exceed speedup threshold p.
claims.poster_quote: Metrics include compilation rate, correctness rate, geometric mean speedup over XLA with regressions floored at 1.0×, and fast-p: the fraction of tasks that are correct and exceed speedup threshold p.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To assess both the robustness and the optimization quality of the generated kernels, we report four primary metrics: (1) The compilation rate [...] (2) The correctness rate [...] (3) geometric mean speedup across all tasks relative to the standard XLA compiler baseline [...] (4) fast-p: the fraction of tasks that both achieve strict functional correctness and exceed a specific speedup threshold p.
claims.reason: Section 3.1, Evaluation Metrics and Methods, explicitly lists the metrics, including compilation rate, correctness rate, geometric mean speedup, and fast-p.

claims.text: Correctness is checked against unoptimized JAX references, generally using absolute and relative tolerances of 10⁻², with selected bf16 workloads relaxed to at most 10⁻¹.
claims.poster_quote: Correctness is checked against unoptimized JAX references, generally using absolute and relative tolerances of 10⁻², with selected bf16 workloads relaxed to at most 10⁻¹.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Numerical equivalence is checked using jnp.allclose with both absolute and relative tolerances set to 10−2 (atol = rtol = 10−2 ) for most cases. To safely account for standard bf16 variance in custom hardware-accelerated math, certain tasks’ tolerance are relaxed to at most 10−1.
claims.reason: Section 3.1, Evaluation Metrics and Methods, confirms correctness is checked against unoptimized JAX references with tolerances of 10⁻², and some bf16 workloads are relaxed to 10⁻¹.

claims.text: XProf measures on-device execution time while excluding host dispatch and compilation overhead.
claims.poster_quote: XProf measures on-device execution time while excluding host dispatch and compilation overhead.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To measure true hardware performance, the harness integrates directly with XProf profiling tool. This allows the system to capture precise on-device execution times while explicitly filtering out host-side JAX dispatch and compilation overheads.
claims.reason: Section 3.1, Evaluation Metrics and Methods, confirms XProf measures on-device execution time while excluding host dispatch and compilation overhead.

claims.text: Methods include Best-of-100 zero-shot generation, five-iteration MaxKernel Auto, five concurrent Auto trajectories for Parallel Search, and Beam Search with width 3, depth 3, two branches per node, and two inner iterations.
claims.poster_quote: Methods include Best-of-100 zero-shot generation, five-iteration MaxKernel Auto, five concurrent Auto trajectories for Parallel Search, and Beam Search with width 3, depth 3, two branches per node, and two inner iterations.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We compare the following four generation methods: • Best-of- 𝑁 (Zero-Shot): Independent zero-shot completions [...] • MaxKernel Auto: A single-trajectory iterative refinement agent restricted to 5 iterations. [...] • MaxKernel Parallel: Executed via 5 concurrent MaxKernel Auto trajectories (5 iterations each). [...] • MaxKernel Beam: A structured, top-𝑘 guided graph search configured with a beam width of 3, a maximum depth of 3, and 2 expansion branches per node.
claims.reason: Section 3.1, Evaluation Metrics and Methods, lists the methods, including Best-of-100 zero-shot, five-iteration MaxKernel Auto, five concurrent Auto trajectories for Parallel Search, and Beam Search with specified parameters.
